title: Chapter 79 – Zhao Yao's Offer
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Zhao Yao]

The letter comes folded inside a laundry bundle, tied with a red thread, and Zhao Yao knows what it says before he opens it.

He has been waiting for it since the day he arrived. The washerwoman who delivers it is a bent gray stranger with chapped hands, who sets the bundle on his cot in Willow Courtyard and says, "Your shirts, young master," in the flat voice of a person reciting a lesson. She does not look at him. She does not wait for a coin. She is gone before he has found his knife.

He cuts the thread. Between the second shirt and the third lies a slip of rice paper, thin as a leaf.

Yao. The house is not finished. The Deacon of the Contribution Hall is a friend of the house, and he will find you. Do as he says. Watch the Pill Hall boy. When the Deacon calls, bring him. If you fail, your brother will pay.

There is no signature. There does not need to be. It is written in the small upright hand of his uncle's steward, the same hand that wrote the household accounts when Zhao Yao was a child, and the last line is underlined twice.

Your brother will pay.

He folds the slip very small. He burns it in the lamp. He watches the edge curl black, and the black run inward, and the last gray flake fall in the dish.

Hui is seven.

He sits for a long time on the edge of the cot with his hands between his knees. The courtyard is quiet. Outside, snow-melt drips from the eaves.

* * *

He is fourteen years old, and he has been a Zhao of Red Ridge for every day of it.

He was born in the long house under the ridge, in the winter when the river froze, to a father who kept the clan's tallies and a mother who sang. He remembers the smell of that house: lamp oil and wet wool and boiled cabbage. He remembers a sister, Lin, two years younger, who had a gap in her teeth and could whistle through it, and who followed him round the yard like a small gray duck.

He remembers the day the Register examiner came.

It was not an official examiner. He knows that now. It was a man in a plain gray robe who said he was from the Azure Cloud Sect, and who was taken to the main hall by Uncle Heng's steward and given tea. The children of the clan were lined up in the yard, all twelve of them, from the youngest to the eldest. The man walked down the line and laid his hand on each head. He said good to one, and no to another, and when he came to Lin he stopped.

He said: Interesting.

She was seven. Zhao Yao was nine.

They took her that night. His father went to the main hall to ask where, and came home with a face like paper, and did not speak for three days. His mother sang no more. On the fourth day, a servant brought a small wooden box to the door, and in it was a lock of hair tied with a red thread, and a note that said the testing was unsuccessful.

He has never learned what that means. He has asked, once, and his father put a hand over his mouth. A month later his father went out to the north terraces with a hoe and did not come back.

The testing.

Uncle Heng's name was on the note. Elder Mu's hand was behind it. And a year later Mu stood in the main hall and the clan was told that the Lin of Green Pine Hill had stolen a Garden, and that every Zhao would be made rich by its return, and that anyone who doubted would be remembered.

He did not doubt. He was twelve, and a coward, and he wanted to be rich.

Then the siege came, and sixty men died in a trench, and Uncle Heng was carried out of the Lin hall in a chair with his face the color of ash. And Zhao Yao, standing in the cold with the other surviving boys of the clan, had thought, with a plain bright wonder that surprised him: He did this. He did all of it.

He had hated them ever since. All of them. Heng, and Mu, and the steward, and the house with its long hall and its quiet servants, and the man in the gray robe who laid a hand on his sister's head. He had hated them with a cold clean patient hatred, a thing he could hold in his hand like a coin.

And he had come here, to the Outer Court of the Azure Cloud Sect, because the Court had said he might, and because it was the only place in the world he could think of where Red Ridge could not reach him.

I was wrong.

* * *

The Contribution Hall is dark at the third watch.

He comes up the side stair, as he was told. He wears his gray tunic and felt wraps. A small clay jar, sealed with wax, hangs from a cord round his neck, and it is cold against his breastbone. The courier had put it in his hands that afternoon, and said only: The Deacon.

He has not opened it.

That is the point he keeps returning to as he climbs. He could have. The wax is a simple press-seal, the sort that comes off with a warm knife. But he is a Zhao, and a Zhao who opens a seal is a Zhao who has been caught, and he has spent two months learning how to be a boy nobody notices.

At the top of the stair, a door stands ajar.

Beyond it is a corridor, narrow and long, and at the end a line of yellow light under another door. The Deacon's office. He knows it. He has seen it from the yard: a single barred window on the second floor, always lit.

He walks to it with soft steps. He stops with his hand raised to knock.

There are voices inside.

He had not expected that. He had thought the Deacon would be alone, at his ledger, as he always is, with his hands folded and his eyes lowered. Instead there are two. One he knows: soft, dry, without color. The other is deeper and slower, and each word is laid down carefully, like a stone on a stone.

"...declined," says the Deacon.

"Declined."

"A pot. A hill pine in black soil. A note: Apply to the Court."

A low breath, which might be a laugh. "He is quick. It is a good answer. It gives nothing and admits nothing and leaves us nowhere to go." The deep voice settles. "How old is he?"

"Ten."

"And you could not buy him."

"He is not a man who can be bought, Master. He is a man who counts." The Deacon's voice is carefully even. "I made the offer you instructed. I named the writ. I named the Inner Sect. He read it and did the sums and came to a conclusion I did not like."

"Which was?"

"That I would move against him either way."

Silence. Zhao Yao stands with his raised hand and his heart beating in his ears. He does not breathe.

"Well," says the deep voice, thoughtfully, "he is not wrong."

Master.

The word goes through him like a cold wire. He has heard it used before, in his uncle's hall, in the mouth of Elder Mu, who was a Pool, and who bowed his head each time he said it. Master was not a title the Zhao used for anyone but Heng. It was a title for the thing above Mu. The thing in the dark, the Blood Shadow's Well, the one who gave orders that came down through three pairs of hands.

He has never seen one. He has never met anyone who has.

"The boy at the Pill Hall interests me," says the deep voice. "I did not expect him to be so careful. I had thought, from the reports, that he was merely lucky. I find that I am corrected." A pause. "Is he blind?"

"He walks into doors."

"Yes. I have been watching him walk into doors." There is something very like amusement in it. "Something has happened to him. Something at the landing. The Hall of Enforcement can find no trace, and neither could I, and I have a better nose than Duan's." The voice drops. "Do you know what it means, when a man who could see goes blind?"

"No, Master."

"It means the thing that let him see has been taken, or spent." A soft click, as of a finger tapping wood. "He is not dangerous now. He is twenty-one years old with a pangolin and a sharp tongue. Do you understand what an opportunity that is?"

"Yes, Master."

"Then why is he not in the cellar?"

The Deacon is silent. Zhao Yao, outside, feels the sweat go cold on the back of his neck.

"Because he is protected," says the Deacon at last. "By the Pill Hall. By Elder Bai. By the Arbiter's attention, which has not yet turned away. A boy who vanishes from the Outer Court in the first month of his trial, with half the Hall watching, is a boy who will be found."

"Not if he is not missed."

"Master?"

"Not if the Court has a reason to forget him." The voice has gone quiet and level. "The boy has a friend. A brother. A cousin from Red Ridge, who was told to watch him. Is the cousin reliable?"

They mean me.

"The Zhao boy is fourteen and hates his own clan," says the Deacon. "He does as he is told because he has a brother. He is afraid. He will bring the Lin boy where I ask."

"Good." A long exhale, almost content. "Then we shall use him. At the new moon after next. I will be here." The deep voice pauses. "I should like to see the child's face when he understands what he has been carrying."

Something moves in the room. A chair scrapes.

Zhao Yao steps back.

* * *

He does not remember going down the stair.

He remembers the cold. He remembers his feet, finding the steps without help. He remembers the courtyard, and a pump handle, and a bucket of snow-melt in which he put his face. He remembers coming up out of it with his heart going like a drum and thinking, with perfect clarity: the Master is inside the Court.

Not outside. Not in Qingshi, or the Gray Peak, or the cold villages under the ridge. Inside. In a room at the end of a corridor in the Contribution Hall, with a voice like a stone laid on a stone. He is a Well. He is, by every account Zhao Yao has ever heard, a man who can cross a courtyard and kill a Foundation cultivator without breaking a sweat. And he has been sitting at a Deacon's desk, in the heart of the Outer Court, for who knows how long.

He wants Lin Jian.

He wants him for something. Not killing, or not yet; Zhao Yao would have heard that word. A use. A vessel. A key. He does not know. He knows only that the Lin boy has a Garden in his blood, and a lock that hums, and that these people will pay anything for them.

And I am the one who is to bring him.

He lifts his face from the bucket. Water runs down his neck.

Hui is seven.

There are two roads, and he has been standing at the fork all night. The first is the one that was drawn for him. He does as he is told. He watches the Pill Hall boy. When the Deacon calls, he brings him, at the new moon after next, to whatever room the Master has chosen. The Master keeps his brother alive. The Master keeps Zhao Yao alive. Perhaps, in a year, there is a house in Qingshi, and a pension, and a quiet.

The second road has no end that he can see.

He thinks of Lin. He thinks of the lock of hair, and the red thread, and the sentence on the note. The testing was unsuccessful. He thinks of the gray man who laid a hand on her head and said interesting. He thinks, with a slow cold clarity that frightens him by its calm: I know what the Master is. I know what he does. I have known since I was nine.

I will not carry another child to it.

He lifts himself off his knees. He dries his face on his sleeve. He stands in the dark courtyard, in the wet, in the cold, with his hands shaking, and makes the first decision of his life that is entirely his own.

* * *

He spends the day doing what he has done for two months: carrying things.

A runner's work is dull and invisible, which is why he took it. Paper to the third clerk. A tray of tea to the fifth. A message to the counter, a bundle to the vault, a bucket of sand for the stairs. He moves through the Contribution Hall like a draft. The clerks do not see him. The disciples in the queue do not see him. Only the Deacon sees him, and then only as one sees a chair.

Today he watches.

He carries a stack of slips to the clerk with ink on his cuffs, a young man named Sun who has been at the Hall three years. Sun takes them without looking up. His brush is going steadily down a column of figures. Zhao Yao stands at his elbow, waiting for the receipt, and sees what he has never looked for before: the ink. Sun's ink is a soft brown, from a green bottle, that sinks into the page as it goes. At the other end of the table, in the Deacon's own hand on the great black book, it lies glossy and hard on top of the paper like a scab.

He writes in something else.

He looks at the Deacon, who stands behind the scale with his hands folded. He looks at the folded hands.

He has seen them tremble. He has told himself it was age.

Sun hands him the receipt. His eyes flick up, once, to Zhao Yao's face, and there is in them, very briefly, something Zhao Yao has not seen there before. Not suspicion. A kind of tired caution, as of a man who has found a stain in a ledger and has been told to say nothing.

"Run along," says Sun, very quietly. "And do not look at the register. It is bad for the eyes."

* * *

He finds the Lin boy in the dead yard behind the Pill Hall the next night.

He has watched him for six days. He knows the schedule. The boy comes out before the bell, in the dark, with a stick in his hand and a small bronze-scaled creature on his collar, and beats a fence post in the snow until his arms shake. Then he goes back. It is a poor way to practice. Zhao Yao has seen the post hit, and missed, and hit. He has seen the boy stop and put a hand against his own ribs, as a man does who is feeling for a wound.

He is blind. The Master was right.

He waits in the shadow of the herb-store wall until the stick has fallen still.

"Lin Jian."

The boy does not start. He turns his head, very slowly, in the dim, and the creature on his collar rises on its scales like a hedgehog. He is small, smaller than Zhao Yao expected, with a plain narrow face and gray eyes that seem too old for it. There is no fear in them. There is only a patient attention, as if he were reading a page.

"Zhao Yao," he says. "Of Willow Courtyard."

"You know me."

"I have watched you watch me." The voice is quiet. "On the stair, on the day of the trial. In the refectory. You are very good at it. I noticed only because you were looking at my feet."

"Your feet?"

"People look at my face, or my hands. You looked at my feet, to see how I walk." A pause. "You wanted to know if I was hurt."

Zhao Yao says nothing. It is, he realizes, exactly right.

"I came to tell you a thing," he says instead. "And to ask for a thing. I would like to say the first before you decide about the second."

"Say it."

"You have no reason to trust me."

"No."

"I am a Zhao of Red Ridge. My uncle raised sixty men against your mother's house. My clan sold the Court a story that your family stole a Garden." He keeps his voice level. "I was told to watch you. I have a letter that says so. I burned it. I will describe it, if you wish."

"I do not need you to."

"No?"

"You are standing in the dark in the snow, fourteen years old, with your hands in your sleeves, to tell me something that could get you killed." The gray eyes hold his. "If you were a spy, you would have come in daylight with a gift."

Zhao Yao laughs. It is a short, harsh, startled sound, and it shocks him.

"Yes," he says. "I would have."

* * *

He tells it plainly. He has rehearsed it all day.

The letter. The jar. The corridor and the lit door, the two voices, the word Master. The new moon after next. He gives the Deacon's words as nearly as he can recall them. The pot with the pine. He is a man who counts. The line about the cellar. He sees the boy's face change at blind, a small tight movement at the corner of the mouth, and at a reason to forget him, a stillness.

"Is he in the Court now?" says Lin Jian, when he has finished.

"He was last night. In the office. I did not see his face."

"The Deacon."

"Mo Lian."

"No." The boy shakes his head slowly. "The other."

"I did not see him." Zhao Yao hesitates. "There was a hood on the chair. A gray cloak. That is all I could see through the crack. But the voice..."

"What about the voice?"

"It was too old," says Zhao Yao, and finds that he has not meant to say it. "Not old in years. Old like a stone. It did not breathe the way a man breathes. It waited between words as if the words had to cross a long distance."

The creature on the boy's collar has gone rigid. It makes a thin dry sound in its throat.

"A wall that walks," says Lin Jian, very quietly, in no tone Zhao Yao can read.

"What?"

"Nothing." He lowers the stick. "I saw him. Two days ago. On the Medicine Valley stair. He stood and looked at me, and put up his hand." The pale face does not change. "I did not know what he was. I had no way to know. I know now."

"What do you mean to do?"

"I do not know." It is said simply. "I am blind, Zhao Yao. You were right. I cannot see Qi. I cannot read a man. I cannot tell a Well from a well-dressed servant. I have a stick, six pins, and a creature that feels the seams of stone." A pause, and then, with a dry flicker that might be humor: "I have a very good ledger."

"That is not a plan."

"No. It is the beginning of one." He tilts his head. "You said you came to ask for something."

Zhao Yao draws a breath.

"I have a brother," he says. "He is seven. He is in Red Ridge, in the care of my uncle's steward, and the steward is a Blood Shadow thread. I was told that if I fail, he pays." The words come hard. "I want him out. Before the new moon after next. I want him in Green Pine Hill, behind your father's gate, under your clan's name, where no one can reach him."

It is a monstrous thing to ask. He knows it as he says it. The Lin clan has just buried forty-nine of its own because of Red Ridge. A Zhao child, any Zhao child, will be the object of every grudge in the valley.

"That is the price," he says. "For what I know. For what I will hear. I will be your ears in the Contribution Hall. I run errands for the clerks; I am in and out of that office twice a day. I will tell you everything. And when the time comes, I will do whatever you ask, short of killing." His voice is shaking now, and he cannot stop it. "That is all I have. It is not much."

The boy is quiet for a long moment.

"I cannot promise it," he says.

Zhao Yao's chest goes cold.

"I can ask. I will ask my father. He is Patriarch, and the decision is his, and the clan has every right to say no." The gray eyes are steady. "But I will tell you what I will tell him. That the boy is seven. That he is not his uncle. That a child who is taken in is a child who grows up in a house that was kind to him." A beat. "I will not lie about what he is. I will not call him a friend of the clan. I will call him a child."

"And if your father says no?"

"Then I will find another way." Lin Jian shifts the stick to his other hand. "I do not give what I cannot keep. You may think less of me for it."

"I do not."

"Good." The boy steps toward him, and for the first time Zhao Yao sees his face clearly in the starlight: twenty-one years old, narrow, unremarkable, tired. "Then we have an arrangement. You will be my ears. I will ask for your brother. We will not tell the Court." A pause. "And you will tell me one thing now, before we part."

"What?"

"The man in the hood. You said you did not see his face." The gray eyes do not leave him. "But you know who is under the Deacon's."

Zhao Yao stares at him.

He had not thought he had said it. He had not even known he knew. But the boy has said it as one reads a figure from a page, and it is true: he has known, since the bucket, since the pump, since the voice behind the door said I made the offer you instructed, and the Deacon's soft dry words had a stiffness in them, a care, as of a man reading from a script.

"The Deacon is not the Deacon," he says. His mouth is dry. "I have watched Mo Lian for two months. He does not blink. He has not once looked at a woman, or a child, or a bowl of food. His hands are always folded, because if they are not, they shake." He draws a breath. "He is not a man. He is a cloak with a man's shape."

"Say it."

"I do not know the word for it. It is a Blood Shadow craft. It is done with a living face." He swallows. "Someone is wearing Deacon Mo Lian."

The creature on the boy's collar makes a small, savage sound, like a kettle.

"He wears Deacon Mo Lian's face," says Zhao Yao.
